title: Philadelphia-Negative MPNs: One Stuck Switch, Three Diseases
summary: Use driver mutations (JAK2, CALR, MPL), blood counts, EPO and marrow findings to separate polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis from each other and from reactive causes.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 34 Hit 4 (PV), Hit 5 (ET and PMF) and Trap 4 (thrombocytosis). Checked against Palandri 2026 (WHO/ICC 2022 PV criteria), Testa 2026, Strzała 2026 and Shao 2025. Hit 4 says JAK2 V617F is present “in essentially all cases”; it is > 95%, with 3–5% carrying exon 12–15 mutations (register flag rv-pv-jak2). Hit 5 gives PMF median survival as ~5 years; Shao 2025 cites 9.2 years (register flag rv-pmf-survival). Not taught: NAP score in PV, “ET usually > 1000” (JAK2 in ET is taught as ≈ 50–60%, matching the reviewer’s ~50%).

objectives: Explain how JAK2, CALR and MPL driver mutations activate signaling in the MPNs.
Apply the WHO/ICC 2022 criteria for polycythemia vera and recognize secondary erythrocytosis.
Apply the essential thrombocythemia criteria, including exclusion of CML and reactive thrombocytosis.
Recognize the blood and marrow features of primary myelofibrosis and its higher leukemic risk.

scenes.title: Thick blood, high platelets, a scarred marrow
scenes.altText: Three patient cards. Patient A: Hb 18.5 g/dL, headaches. Patient B: platelets 650 × 10⁹/L, found on a routine CBC. Patient C: anemia, big spleen, teardrop cells on the smear. A shared token: “BCR::ABL1 negative.” Question token: “Same engine, three diseases — or not a cancer at all?” The cartoon scientist looks between them.

cues.text: Three patients. One has thick blood, one has a very high platelet count, and one has a big spleen with teardrop-shaped red cells.
None of them has the BCR::ABL1 fusion of chronic myeloid leukemia. They may have the Philadelphia-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms.
Or they may have an ordinary reaction to something else. Driver mutations and diagnostic criteria tell the difference.

props.label: Same engine, three diseases — or a reaction?

scenes.title: One engine, three drivers
scenes.altText: A JAK2 signaling token normally waits for a key (EPO or TPO binding its receptor). A mutation token — JAK2 V617F — switches it on with no key. Two more driver tokens appear: CALR (mutant calreticulin activates the MPL receptor) and MPL. A driver-frequency table builds as cards: PV — JAK2 V617F > 95%, other JAK2 (exons 12–15) 3–5%; ET — JAK2 ≈ 50–60%, CALR 20–25%, MPL ≈ 5%, triple-negative ≈ 10%; PMF — JAK2 ≈ 50–60%, CALR 25–30%, MPL ≈ 5%, triple-negative 5–10%.

cues.text: Blood-cell production is switched on when hormones such as erythropoietin or thrombopoietin bind their receptors and activate the JAK2 signaling enzyme.
The JAK2 V617F mutation keeps JAK2 switched on without the hormone. The marrow overproduces, even when the body does not need more cells.
Two other drivers do the same through the thrombopoietin receptor: mutant calreticulin, CALR, and mutations in the receptor itself, MPL.
In polycythemia vera, more than 95 percent carry JAK2 V617F, and most of the rest carry other JAK2 mutations, in exons 12 to 15.
In essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis, about half to 60 percent carry JAK2; CALR and MPL make up much of the rest, and some are triple-negative.

scenes.title: Polycythemia vera — or a reason to be red?
scenes.altText: A criteria card (WHO/ICC 2022) builds for PV. Major: Hb > 16.5 (men) / > 16.0 (women) g/dL or Hct > 49% / 48% or increased red-cell mass; marrow hypercellular with trilineage growth (panmyelosis); JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12–15 mutation. Minor: low serum EPO. A secondary-erythrocytosis card: hypoxia (lung disease, smoking, sleep apnea), EPO-secreting tumors, testosterone, SGLT2 inhibitors, diuretics — usually with normal or high EPO. Patient A: Hb 18.5, EPO suppressed, JAK2 V617F → PV.

cues.text: Polycythemia vera needs a high red-cell value: hemoglobin above 16.5 in men or 16.0 in women, or hematocrit above 49 or 48 percent, or a raised red-cell mass.
Plus a marrow that is busy in all three lines, called panmyelosis, and a JAK2 mutation: V617F, or one in exons 12 to 15.
A low erythropoietin level supports PV. The clone makes red cells without being asked, so the kidney turns its own signal down.
High hemoglobin has ordinary causes too: low oxygen from lung disease, smoking or sleep apnea, tumors making erythropoietin, testosterone, some diabetes drugs and diuretics.
Patient A has hemoglobin 18.5, a suppressed erythropoietin and JAK2 V617F. That fits polycythemia vera.

scenes.title: ET and PMF: platelets, marrow and scars
scenes.altText: An ET card: platelets persistently ≥ 450 × 10⁹/L; marrow with increased large mature megakaryocytes; not meeting criteria for CML (BCR::ABL1), PV, PMF or MDS; driver mutation (JAK2, CALR, MPL) — or another clonal marker or no evidence of reactive thrombocytosis. Patient B: platelets 650, CALR positive, BCR::ABL1 negative → ET. A PMF card: teardrop cells, leukoerythroblastosis (nucleated RBCs and immature granulocytes), splenomegaly, reticulin/collagen fibrosis; minor criteria: anemia, WBC ≥ 11 × 10⁹/L, palpable spleen, raised LDH; prefibrotic PMF can mimic ET. Outlook tokens: AML transformation ≈ 20% PMF vs ≈ 4% PV vs ≈ 1% ET; median survival in PMF ≈ 9 years in one large series.

cues.text: Essential thrombocythemia needs a persistent platelet count of at least 450, a marrow full of large, mature megakaryocytes, and no other myeloid neoplasm, including CML.
Then a driver mutation, or another clonal marker, or no evidence that the high platelets are a reaction to something else. Patient B is CALR-positive and BCR::ABL1-negative: ET.
Primary myelofibrosis scars the marrow. Red cells squeezed out of the fibrotic marrow become teardrops, and immature cells leak into the blood: leukoerythroblastosis.
Supporting findings are anemia, a white count of 11 or more, a palpable spleen and a raised LDH. Early, prefibrotic myelofibrosis can look like ET.
Myelofibrosis carries the highest risk of turning into acute leukemia, about 20 percent, versus about 4 percent in PV and 1 percent in ET.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “Platelets 600 = ET” (✓ exclude CML with BCR::ABL1, other neoplasms and reactive causes first); “JAK2 V617F negative rules out PV” (✓ 3–5% have JAK2 exon 12–15 mutations); “ET and PMF are JAK2 diseases” (✓ JAK2 in only about 50–60%; the rest CALR, MPL or triple-negative).

cues.text: Trap one: a platelet count of 600 means ET. Not until CML is excluded with BCR::ABL1 testing, along with other neoplasms and reactive causes.
Trap two: a negative JAK2 V617F test rules out PV. No. Three to five percent carry JAK2 mutations in exons 12 to 15 instead.
Trap three: ET and myelofibrosis are JAK2 diseases. Only about half to 60 percent are; CALR, MPL or no known driver account for the rest.

scenes.title: One stuck switch, three outputs
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “One stuck switch, three outputs.” A JAK–STAT switch stuck ON feeds three pipes: red cells (PV — almost always JAK2), platelets (ET — JAK2, CALR or MPL), fibrosis (PMF — the same drivers, plus scarring). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: one stuck switch, three outputs. The same switched-on signaling can mainly raise red cells in PV, platelets in ET, or scar the marrow in myelofibrosis.

Where it breaks: the same mutation can cause different diseases; prefibrotic myelofibrosis overlaps with ET; driver mutations also appear in healthy older people with clonal hematopoiesis; and criteria need marrow findings, not just a mutation.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “PV: Hb > 16.5/16.0 + panmyelosis + JAK2 (V617F > 95%, exon 12–15 3–5%) · low EPO”, “ET: plt ≥ 450 + megakaryocytes + exclude CML/reactive · PMF: fibrosis, teardrops, leukoerythroblastosis”.

cues.text: Diagnose the Philadelphia-negative MPNs with blood counts, marrow findings and a driver mutation — JAK2 in nearly all PV, JAK2, CALR or MPL in ET and myelofibrosis — after excluding CML and reactive causes.

props.label: PV: Hb > 16.5/16.0 + panmyelosis + JAK2 (V617F > 95%, exon 12–15 3–5%) · low EPO
ET: plt ≥ 450 + megakaryocytes + exclude CML/reactive · PMF: fibrosis, teardrops

explanation.what: Plain language: in these blood cancers, a stuck “on” switch makes the marrow overproduce red cells, platelets or scar tissue. Scientific terms: Philadelphia-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (PV, ET, PMF), JAK2 V617F, JAK2 exon 12–15 mutations, CALR, MPL, triple-negative, panmyelosis, leukoerythroblastosis, prefibrotic and overt PMF.
explanation.why: JAK2 V617F causes constitutive JAK2 activation without EPO or TPO binding; mutant CALR activates the MPL (TPO) receptor; MPL mutations activate it directly. Autonomous red-cell production suppresses EPO.
explanation.measure: PV (WHO/ICC 2022): Hb > 16.5/16.0 g/dL or Hct > 49/48% or increased red-cell mass; marrow panmyelosis; JAK2 V617F or exon 12–15; minor: low EPO. ET: platelets ≥ 450 × 10⁹/L, characteristic megakaryocytes, exclusion of other myeloid neoplasms, driver mutation (minor: clonal marker or no reactive thrombocytosis). PMF minor criteria: anemia, WBC ≥ 11 × 10⁹/L, palpable spleen, raised LDH (plus leukoerythroblastosis in overt PMF).
explanation.differs: PV vs secondary erythrocytosis (EPO, hypoxia, drugs); ET vs reactive thrombocytosis and CML (BCR::ABL1); ET vs prefibrotic PMF (marrow morphology).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: low EPO + JAK2 = PV; JAK2 V617F-negative PV with exon 12; CALR-positive ET; teardrops and leukoerythroblastosis = PMF; always exclude BCR::ABL1.

mnemonic.explanation: JAK–STAT signaling stuck on raises red cells (PV), platelets (ET) or drives fibrosis (PMF).
mnemonic.limitation: The same mutation can cause different diseases; prefibrotic PMF overlaps ET; drivers also occur in clonal hematopoiesis; criteria need marrow findings.

analogyLimitations: The switch and pipes are schematic.
CML, mastocytosis and MPN treatment are not covered here.
takeaway: Diagnose the Philadelphia-negative MPNs with blood counts, marrow findings and a driver mutation — JAK2 in nearly all PV, JAK2, CALR or MPL in ET and myelofibrosis — after excluding CML and reactive causes.

questions.stem: A woman has Hb 17.4 g/dL, a low serum EPO and a hypercellular marrow with trilineage growth. JAK2 V617F is negative. What is the best next test?

options.rationale: Correct. 3–5% of PV carry non-V617F JAK2 mutations, mostly in exon 12.

options.text: Rule out PV and diagnose secondary erythrocytosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Low EPO and panmyelosis still point to PV; a negative V617F test does not exclude it.
Incorrect. CML is not suggested by isolated erythrocytosis with low EPO.
Incorrect. Ferritin does not diagnose PV.

questions.stem: Platelets are 680 × 10⁹/L on repeated counts. Before diagnosing essential thrombocythemia, which test is essential?

options.rationale: Correct. ET requires that criteria for CML and other myeloid neoplasms are not met.
Incorrect. EPO is a minor criterion for PV, not ET.
Incorrect. It does not help classify thrombocytosis.

options.text: None — a platelet count ≥ 450 is diagnostic
options.rationale: Incorrect. A high count alone does not distinguish ET from reactive or other neoplastic causes.

questions.stem: An anemic patient has splenomegaly, teardrop cells, nucleated red cells and myelocytes on the smear, and a CALR mutation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Correct. Teardrops, leukoerythroblastosis, splenomegaly and a driver mutation fit PMF.
Incorrect. ET lacks leukoerythroblastosis and marrow fibrosis.
Incorrect. PV causes erythrocytosis, not anemia with fibrosis at presentation.
Incorrect. A CALR mutation indicates a clonal neoplasm.

PV criteria (Hb/Hct/RCM, panmyelosis, JAK2 V617F or exon 12–15; low EPO) and secondary erythrocytosis causes.
ET criteria: platelets ≥ 450, megakaryocytes, exclusion of other myeloid neoplasms incl. CML, driver or clonal marker or no reactive cause.
PMF features, minor criteria, AML risk 20/4/1%, median survival 9.2 years.
NAP elevated in 80% of PV; ET platelets usually > 1000; reactive causes of thrombocytosis (iron deficiency, infection, inflammation).
